t: Maximum Number of Alloys — Binary Search per Machine
o: For a fixed machine, the cost of producing t alloys is Σ_j max(0, composition[j]·t − stock[j])·cost[j], which is monotonically non-decreasing in t (each term grows). So for each machine binary-search the largest affordable t, and take the max over machines. Example 2: machine 2 barely needs metal 3 thanks to stock 100, so t=5 fits budget 15.
k: Cost is monotone in t ⇒ binary search the answer per machine.

a.i: feasible(machine, t) computes purchase cost with 64-bit arithmetic; binary search t over [0, high] where high safely bounds budget/min-cost (e.g., 2·10^8).
s: For each machine, binary search the maximum t with cost(t) ≤ budget.
cost(t) = Σ max(0, comp[j]·t − stock[j]) · cost[j].
a.t: O(k · n · log(maxT)) — k machines × ~28 binary-search steps × O(n) cost evaluation

w: Overflow is the main trap: comp[j]·t reaches 100 × 2·10^8 = 2·10^10, so use 64-bit (long long / long; JS numbers are safe up to 2^53 here). Early-exit the cost sum once it exceeds budget. Follow-up: what if alloys could mix machines?
